node.label: Julia Cherry Spruill
node.date_label: Women’s social history in colonial America · 1938
node.description: Investigates women’s everyday life, institutions, work and public activity in the colonial South through varied documentary evidence. Later reissues and public interpretation renew use of her work while exposing limits in whose lives become sustained research questions.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Women’s Life and Work in the Southern Colonies (1938); later reissues associated with Anne Firor Scott show that the field’s expansion also involved renewed attention to earlier scholarship.
node.scope_note: Richter’s complete 1999 review mediates Spruill’s shift from attitudes to empirical groundwork and her distinction between prescribed reading and actual behavior. The book examines status and regional differences, but mentions Black and Native women without sustained questions about their life and work, in Richter’s assessment. Scott’s 1972 and 1998 introductions are editorial reception; Colonial Williamsburg use is documented, while Richter’s own proposed slavery research remains an intention. Earlier methods are not membership in postwar social history, and friendship with Beard does not prove transmission.

sources.title: Natalie Zemon Davis, Women on the Margins: Three Seventeenth-Century Lives (1995), consulted third printing/first paperback (1997), selected primary passages.
sources.citation: Natalie Zemon Davis, Women on the Margins: Three Seventeenth-Century Lives (1995), consulted third printing/first paperback (1997), selected primary passages.

verification.note: Public OCR read: title/edition; complete prologue pp. 1–4, conclusion pp. 203–216 and acknowledgments pp. 340–344; selected Glikl opening pp. 6–8 and conclusion notes 1–8/start of 9. Main chapters and remaining notes not fully read. Prologue is an imagined October 1994 dialogue. Certeau and Foucault are explicit resources; editions/translations and collaboration are discussed. Original manuscripts, Glikl editions and clinical work uncollated. Pappenheim was treated by Breuer, not Freud; Davis’s reconstruction of her likely feelings is conjectural. This primary selection supplements, rather than retroactively upgrades, the existing catalogue record.

sources.title: Ivy Pinchbeck: Women Workers and the Industrial Revolution
sources.citation: Ivy Pinchbeck, Women Workers and the Industrial Revolution, 1750–1850 (George Routledge & Sons, 1930; reprint with new preface, Frank Cass, 1969).

verification.note: Additional publisher-preview reading: complete original preface vi, complete introduction pp. 1–5, 1969 reprint preface signed October 1968, and opening chapter I p. 7. Distinguishes occupational visibility, family wages, training, marital status, disruption and claimed eventual gains. Names Knowles, Power, scholarship support and George. The later preface proposes post-1850 research rather than supplying it. Remaining occupational chapters and conclusion unread; optimistic generalization is attributed, not independently proven. Previous scope: Publisher-distributed preview: copyright page confirms 1930 original and 1969 reprint; original preface p. vi acknowledges Eileen Power’s research direction and Lilian Knowles’s earlier guidance; introduction pp. 1–2 addresses women’s work before industrialization. Full book and later reception not audited.

sources.title: Julie Richter, review of Julia Cherry Spruill, Women’s Life and Work in the Southern Colonies, H-SAWH, March 1999.
sources.citation: Julie Richter, review of Julia Cherry Spruill, Women’s Life and Work in the Southern Colonies, H-SAWH, March 1999.

verification.note: Complete review read from original H-Net HTML obtained with curl after browser access failed. Quotes Spruill’s original preface and p. 208, describes Scott’s reissue introduction, and documents Colonial Williamsburg use. Criticism concerns questions not asked about Black and Native women, not their total absence. Richter’s planned use for a slavery study is future intent. Book, original preface and Scott introductions remain mediated; friendship with Beard does not establish methodological transmission.
